summary: This Standards Track document allocates TLS code points so client certificates can use RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures in TLS 1.3. This removes an obstacle for some deployments moving to TLS 1.3.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old ID cards only work with an old kind of scanner. This adds the old scanner setting back so those cards still work with the new system.

questions: rsa pkcs1 v1.5 client certificates tls 1.3
subtitle: Three TLS 1.3 code points so old hardware keys can still sign client certificate handshakes.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 dropped RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 in CertificateVerify, but many TPMs and other hardware devices holding client certificate keys cannot produce the RSASSA-PSS signatures TLS 1.3 requires, so those deployments are stuck on TLS 1.2.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new SignatureScheme values for RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, usable only in the client CertificateVerify message.
tldr.outcome: Servers can opt in to accept these legacy client signatures, which unblocks TLS 1.3 for such clients. Implementations SHOULD disable the code points by default.

today: RFC 9963 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2026. The unit metadata shows it neither obsoletes nor updates another RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Legacy Keys Block TLS 1.3
sections.content:
RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) removed RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 from CertificateVerify messages in favor of RSASSA-PSS. Some legacy hardware cryptographic devices lack RSASSA-PSS. This is uncommon in servers but happens with TLS clients using client certificates.

The example given is the Trusted Platform Module (TPM). TPM specifications before 2.0 did not define RSASSA-PSS. TPM 2.0 includes it, but only TPM 2.0 devices compatible with US FIPS 186-4 can be relied on to use a salt length equal to the digest length, as TLS 1.3 requires.
sections.plainLanguage: New locks need a special key shape, but some old keys cannot be made that shape, so the people carrying them stay out.

sections.title: The Cost of Staying on TLS 1.2
sections.content:
Staying on TLS 1.2 leaks the client certificate to network attackers and prevents protection against retroactive decryption by an attacker with a quantum computer (see RFC 9954).

There is also a negotiation problem. TLS agrees on a protocol version before client certificates are exchanged. A client sends its ClientHello without knowing whether the server will ask for a legacy key, and the server picks a version and sends a CertificateRequest without knowing whether the client will answer with one. If both pick TLS 1.3 and the client then has a legacy key, the connection fails, where it worked on TLS 1.2 before.

The recovery options are poor: one side must disable TLS 1.3 globally, which hurts unaffected connections, or the client must implement an external fallback, which breaks TLS's security analysis and may introduce vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: If the old key holders just stay with the old system, they lose privacy. And if the two sides guess wrong about the key, the door slams shut halfway through.

sections.title: The New SignatureScheme Values
sections.content:
Three values are added to SignatureScheme: rsa_pkcs1_sha256_legacy (0x0420), rsa_pkcs1_sha384_legacy (0x0520) and rsa_pkcs1_sha512_legacy (0x0620). Each means RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (RFC 8017) with the stated hash from the Secure Hash Standard.

They are defined only for signatures in the client CertificateVerify message. A server that wants to advertise RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 in its certificates should use the existing rsa_pkcs1_* constants from RFC 8446.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three new labels for the old key type, one for each size of fingerprint the key can use. They are only for people showing ID, not for the building's own ID.

sections.title: Who May Offer and Accept Them
sections.content:
Clients MUST NOT advertise these values in the signature_algorithms extension of the ClientHello, and MUST NOT accept them in the server CertificateVerify message.

Servers that want to support clients with legacy RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5-only keys MAY send these values in the signature_algorithms extension of the CertificateRequest and accept them in the client CertificateVerify. Servers MUST NOT accept them if they were not offered in the CertificateRequest.

Clients with such keys MAY use them if offered. Clients SHOULD NOT use them with keys that support RSASSA-PSS, although that may be hard to determine, since testing a key might show a message to the user or have other side effects. TLS implementations SHOULD disable these code points by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the guard at the door may say the old key shape is welcome. Visitors do not ask for it, and anyone with a modern key should use that instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The reasoning in Section 1 does not apply to server keys, so these code points are forbidden for server certificates. RSASSA-PSS continues to be required for TLS 1.3 servers using RSA keys, which limits the impact to cases where it is needed to unblock deployment.

Implemented incorrectly, RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 admits signature forgeries. Implementations MUST follow Section 8.2 of RFC 8017. In particular, clients MUST include the mandatory NULL parameter in the DigestInfo structure and produce valid DER encoding, and servers MUST reject signatures that do not meet these requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The old key shape is easy to fake if checkers are sloppy, so everyone must follow the exact rules, and the servers themselves must keep using the newer kind.

sections.title: IANA Registry Entries
sections.content: IANA created the three entries in the "TLS SignatureScheme" registry. The "Recommended" column is set to N and the "Reference" column points to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of allowed labels now includes the three new ones, marked as not recommended.
